title: Meeting Time Planner: Times That Align
description: Find when local times align across cities with the Meeting Time Planner — daylight-saving rules included. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 9:00 a.m. in New York is 2:00 p.m. in London and 7:30 p.m. in Mumbai — a workable three-continent slot that survives most of the year, and the planner shows you the weeks when it does not.
quick_answer: The Meeting Time Planner lines up several locations' local clocks for a candidate time so you can see when a call actually works for everyone. Add the cities, pick a time, and compare everyone's clock — daylight-saving rules included, since changeover weeks are where recurring meetings die.

Three generations, three continents: the planner finds the kind hour — awake for the kids, not midnight for the grandparents.
Proposing a time inside everyone's workday is basic courtesy made visible. Send the planner's result as the receipt.
A launch at 9:00 New York is 14:00 London and 19:30 Mumbai — prime time or dead air, depending on the audience you wanted.

9:00 New York (winter, EST) = 14:00 UTC = 14:00 London, 15:00 Berlin, 19:30 Mumbai. In summer New York's 9:00 becomes 13:00 UTC and London stays 14:00 (BST) — the slot survives, which is why it is a classic.

Add Sydney and the same slot lands at 1:00 a.m. (winter, AEDT next day). No single hour flatters four continents — rotate the pain or split the meeting; the planner makes the cost explicit instead of surprising.

popular_table.intro: A winter weekday, 9:00 a.m. New York rendered everywhere — computed with standard-time offsets; the planner applies each city's live rules.
popular_table.note: Half-hour offsets (Mumbai) and date-line flips (Sydney) are why planners exist. DST weeks shift some rows by an hour — the planner's rules account for the date you pick.

faq: Yes — the planner applies each location's daylight-saving rules for the date, which is exactly the feature spreadsheets lack and changeover weeks punish.
How many cities can I add?
Several — enough for a genuinely global team. Beyond six or so, the overlap usually vanishes and the tool's honest answer is to rotate times or split the call.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — cities are typed, never detected. Your location is not a participant unless you add it.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Cities resolve via open geocoding; zone rules come from the tz database, the same source your calendar uses — disagreements are rare and usually vintage.
